drills.q: Why is a conversion-probability model the wrong tool for deciding who to target with a promotion?
drills.a: It predicts P(convert|X), which is high for both sure things (convert regardless) and persuadables (convert because of treatment) -- it can't distinguish them, so targeting off it wastes spend on sure things.
tau(x) = E[Y(1)-Y(0)|X=x] -- the expected difference between a unit's potential outcome under treatment and under control, conditional on its features.

drills.q: What's the main weakness of the two-model (T-learner) uplift approach?
drills.a: The treated and control models are fit independently and can have different bias/variance behavior; subtracting two independently-noisy models can amplify noise rather than cancel it, especially with imbalanced arm sizes.

drills.q: What assumption does difference-in-differences rely on, and why is it fundamentally untestable?
drills.a: Parallel trends -- absent treatment, the treated and control groups' outcomes would have moved together. Untestable because it's a claim about an unobserved counterfactual after treatment; you can only support it with pre-treatment trend evidence and placebo tests.

drills.q: What is propensity score matching's core assumption, and name a real critique of the method.
drills.a: Unconfoundedness/ignorability: conditional on measured covariates, treatment is as good as random (no unmeasured confounders) -- unfalsifiable. King & Nielsen (2019) showed matching on a single propensity score can increase covariate imbalance and model dependence versus full/exact matching in some regimes.

drills.q: Explain the exclusion restriction for instrumental variables with a marketing example.
drills.a: The instrument must affect the outcome ONLY through treatment. Example: an ad-server outage shifting who sees an ad, used as an instrument for exposure -- broken if the outage also correlates with a site-wide issue that independently affects purchasing, giving the instrument a second pathway to the outcome.

drills.q: How do causal forests differ from standard random forests?
drills.a: Standard forests split to reduce outcome prediction error. Causal forests split to maximize heterogeneity in the ESTIMATED TREATMENT EFFECT across leaves, using honest splitting (disjoint samples for choosing splits vs estimating effects) to give asymptotically valid confidence intervals on tau(x).

drills.q: Why can't you evaluate an uplift model with ordinary classification AUC?
drills.a: There's no single ground-truth uplift label per individual to score against (you never observe both potential outcomes for one person). Instead use the Qini curve / uplift AUC on a randomized holdout, which measures cumulative incremental conversions within top-k ranked slices by comparing treated vs control conversion rates.

drills.q: Legal has blocked withholding personalization from any user, so you can't run a clean randomized holdout to measure a new email campaign's causal lift. Design a measurement plan.
drills.a: First push to get even a small (e.g. 5%) holdout approved -- usually defensible and far superior to any observational method. If truly blocked, fall back to a geo-level staggered rollout, estimating lift via DiD or synthetic control comparing rolled-out vs not-yet-rolled-out markets, checking pre-period parallel trends. Use PSM only as a secondary sensitivity check, flagging its unconfoundedness assumption as the weak link, not the primary estimate.

drills.q: A colleague wants to target retention offers using a churn-propensity model's output directly. What's the flaw, and what's a 'sleeping dog' in this context?
drills.a: The model predicts P(churn|X), not the effect of the offer -- some high-churn-propensity users will leave regardless (wasted spend) and some low-propensity users might be exactly who the offer would save. A sleeping dog here is a user for whom the retention offer actually INCREASES churn (e.g. an email reminding an inattentive customer they have a subscription, prompting cancellation) -- only an uplift/CATE model can surface this negative-effect segment.
